13.t: Working with data: what the nephron keeps
q: Calculate the percentage of filtered water that is reabsorbed.
Explain why almost no protein is filtered.
Proteins are too large to pass through the basement membrane and the gaps between podocytes in the glomerulus (ultrafiltration).
Explain why a healthy person has no glucose in their urine.
All filtered glucose is reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule, by co-transport with sodium ions.
Urea rises from 0.31 g dm⁻³ in the filtrate to 18.7 g dm⁻³ in urine. Calculate the increase and explain how it happens.
18.7 / 0.31 = 60 times. Over 99% of the water is reabsorbed but about half the urea stays in the tubule, so it becomes concentrated.
A person with untreated diabetes has glucose in their urine and passes more urine. Explain both.
Blood glucose is so high that the carriers are saturated, so some glucose stays in the filtrate. This lowers the water potential of the filtrate, so less water is reabsorbed by osmosis.

19.t: Working with data: drinking and urine
q: Calculate how many times the urine flow increased at its peak after drinking water.
Describe the changes after drinking water.
Flow rises to a peak at about 60 min (300), then falls back almost to the starting level by 150–180 min.
Explain these changes in terms of ADH and aquaporins.

The water lowers the solute concentration of the blood. Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect this, so less ADH is released by the pituitary. Fewer aquaporins in the collecting duct, so less water is reabsorbed: large, dilute urine.
Explain why the salt solution caused almost no change.
It has the same solute concentration as blood, so osmoreceptors are not stimulated and ADH stays the same; the extra volume is lost slowly.
Predict the urine flow if the student had sweated heavily and drunk nothing. Explain.
Flow would fall below 50 and urine would be concentrated: more ADH, more aquaporins, more water reabsorbed.

26.t: Working with data: blood flow in exercise
q: Calculate the percentage of cardiac output that goes to skeletal muscle at rest and in hard exercise.
Calculate how many times cardiac output increased.
Explain how blood flow to the gut and kidneys is reduced.
Sympathetic nerves and adrenaline cause vasoconstriction: smooth muscle in the walls of the arterioles supplying them contracts.
Explain why blood flow to the skin rises during hard exercise.
Respiration releases a lot of heat; skin arterioles dilate so heat is lost by radiation and by evaporation of sweat.
Explain why blood flow to the brain stays the same.
The brain needs a steady supply of glucose and oxygen and cannot store them, so its flow is kept constant whatever the activity.
